name: Colin Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential and your name won't be on it. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker with a contractor that the power companies hire up in the hills, where wildfires are a big worry. Most of our work right now is fire-proofing the lines: swapping old wooden poles for steel ones and putting up covered wire so a branch can't spark a fire. I'm usually on the ground running the winch and the digger, and they let me climb on the easier jobs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being out in the forest, and I like that the work actually stops fires, you can feel good about that. What wears me out is being the least experienced guy on a crew of lifers, I make rookie mistakes and they don't let me forget it. Also the early starts, we're on the road by half five some days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's a lot of hype in everything these days. But I'd also say I still use it every day, so it's not nothing. I'd say that at work and maybe post something short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan doesn't change. Get my ticket, keep building my weekend tree business, and one day run my own small line crew for farms and ranches with private poles. AI's already my secretary, my bookkeeper and my quote-writer, and I didn't have to hire anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I've got about three months saved, and I'd put a chunk of my weekend money towards a better trailer for the chainsaws. I'd keep using AI for the paperwork side, quotes, invoices, scheduling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually, nothing's getting in my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the weekend tree business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trim and fell trees for people on their own land, away from the power lines, that's the rule. Mostly old couples and small farms who can't do it themselves. I started it last year with a used chainsaw and my dad's old trailer, and now I do two or three jobs a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe that people waste money on hype instead of good tools. But that's their business, literally.

S0.say: I'd say there's a lot of hype in everything, but I still use AI every day, so it's not nothing. I'd say that at work and maybe in a short post.
S0.think: It means my plan doesn't change: get my ticket, grow my weekend tree business and one day run my own small crew for private lines. AI is already my secretary, bookkeeper and quote-writer.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal with about three months of savings, and puts part of his weekend income towards a better chainsaw trailer. Keeps using AI daily for quotes, invoices and scheduling.
S0.feel: Calm and even pleased, since nothing is in his way.
S0.quote: AI's already my secretary, my bookkeeper and my quote-writer, and I didn't have to hire anybody.
S0.fieldNote: Colin already thinks like a small business owner, and AI sits comfortably in his routine as unpaid office help. He's careful to say he keeps his tree work away from power lines, which suggests he takes the rules seriously. His long goal is a crew of his own serving farms and ranches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. I'd say the government should stay out of the way and let companies and people figure it out. Apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. Fire-proofing the lines will need people for years, and my side business gets cheaper to run with better software. The guys complaining about AI on my crew are the same ones who still pay someone to do their taxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using whatever new tools the contractor brings in from day one, probably drones for checking poles and AI for planning. I'd invest in a small stump grinder for the tree business, maybe four thousand, and use AI to market it. I'd still keep my savings above two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit fired up. It feels like a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dale. He's been climbing for twenty-five years and he's the best I've seen, but he won't touch a phone app. If they start judging people on the tablet, Dale's going to feel insulted, and he'd have every right. I'd try to help him quietly, without making it a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said four thousand on a stump grinder. Isn't that a lot of your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's more than a month's worth, yeah. I'd buy it used and pay it off with the jobs it brings in, I've already got three people asking. If nobody books it, I'd sell it, they hold their value.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to work and learn, and the government should stay out of the way. Apprenticeships, not handouts.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because fire-proofing lines will need people for years and my side business gets cheaper to run. The crew members complaining about AI still pay someone to do their taxes.
S1.do: Uses the contractor's new drones and planning tools from the first day. Buys a used stump grinder for about four thousand for his tree business, markets it with AI and keeps savings above two months.
S1.feel: Calm and fired up, like a race he can win.
S1.quote: The guys complaining about AI on my crew are the same ones who still pay someone to do their taxes.
S1.fieldNote: Colin sees steady disruption as a competition he's well placed for, and he's willing to put real money into equipment. His free-market views are sharp, but he's gentle about the older climber who won't use apps. He has a plan B for the grinder purchase, which shows his risk-taking is calculated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so stop whining and get moving. I'd tell people that this is when you find out who can adapt. But I'd also say the big companies shouldn't get special deals from the government to make it go faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared, even though I wouldn't admit it at work. If robots can fell trees and climb poles in two years, my day job and my side business both go. My whole plan was to be the boss of a small crew. Now the crew might be three robots and me with a laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. In the first month I'd look into leasing or buying one of the first tree-cutting or climbing robots, even a cheap early one, and running it for clients myself. I'd use the savings and probably sell my truck for something cheaper to fund it, and I'd use AI every night to learn how to run and fix the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Scared, but scared and busy, which beats scared and sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rachel say about selling the truck to buy a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd think I've lost my mind. She's a hairdresser, she rents a chair in a salon, and she's careful with money. But she'd also say, you've always been the one who jumps first, so jump properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your plans with Rachel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've been talking about getting engaged next year. In this picture, I'd still want to, but I'd want to wait till I knew if the robot gamble worked. I wouldn't ask her to marry a man with no plan.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening, so stop whining and get moving, because this is when you find out who can adapt. But big companies shouldn't get special government deals to speed it up.
S2.think: I'd be scared, though I wouldn't admit it at work, because my day job and my side business both go. My plan was to run a small crew, and now the crew might be three robots and me with a laptop.
S2.do: Looks into leasing or buying an early tree-cutting or climbing robot within the first month and runs it for clients himself. Funds it from savings and by trading his truck for a cheaper one, using AI nightly to learn the machine.
S2.feel: Anxious, scared but busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: My whole plan was to be the boss of a small crew. Now the crew might be three robots and me with a laptop.
S2.fieldNote: Colin's response to the fastest picture is to become the owner of the machine rather than its victim. Privately he's frightened, which he hides at work behind tough talk. He'd delay getting engaged until he knew whether his gamble had paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time if you're not lazy. Learn the new tools, save some money, think about where you want to be. I'd tell the younger guys to stop waiting for someone to tell them what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me, I think. I'd get my ticket, grow the tree business, and by year three or four I could have money saved for a robot or two. Then I'd be the guy farmers call to bring the robot and make sure it doesn't wreck their fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder than ever, aiming for six months plus a separate fund for equipment. I'd keep the tree business going and add stump grinding. By year two I'd be watching which robot makers are actually any good, and I'd buy in early, before prices go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still a big thing, but I'd feel like I'm steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make sure the robot doesn't wreck the fence. Is that the job you'd be selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much. People out here don't trust a machine on its own on their land. They'll trust a machine if they know the guy standing next to it went to school with their son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your crew would see you as part of the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them, yeah, Dale for sure. But I'd rather have the robot and the work than have no robot and no work. I'd try to hire guys from the old crew to help me run it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty of time if you're not lazy: learn the tools, save some money and think about where you want to be. Younger guys should stop waiting to be told what to do.
S3.think: Five years is good for me: I'd get my ticket, grow the tree business and save for a robot or two by year three or four. Then farmers call me to bring the robot and look after it.
S3.do: Saves towards six months plus a separate equipment fund, and adds stump grinding to his tree business. Watches robot makers from year two and buys in early before prices rise.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but feeling like he's steering.
S3.quote: They'll trust a machine if they know the guy standing next to it went to school with their son.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Colin plans to own robots and sell local trust alongside them. He accepts some of his crew might see him as part of the problem and would try to hire them. His self-reliance shows in pushing younger workers to act without waiting for instructions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with a bit of drive. Learn a trade, learn the machines, start something of your own. I'd say it to my cousins and the younger apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel good about it. In ten years I could have my own small crew with a couple of robots doing the heavy work and me running the business. I'd rather own one robot than be replaced by somebody else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my ticket, keep growing the tree work and save for the first robot by year five or six. I'd also look at a part-time business course so I know how to run payroll and contracts properly. And I'd ask Rachel to marry me next year like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask Rachel to marry you next year. Does ten years change family plans in any other way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want kids in a few years, and I'd want them to grow up seeing their dad run something. I don't want my kids to think work is something that just happens to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that a lot of people around here won't adapt in time, and the government will try to fix it with handouts. I'd rather see the money go into apprenticeships and helping small businesses buy the machines. Then you've got owners, not just people waiting for a cheque.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with drive: learn a trade, learn the machines and start something of your own. I'd say it to my cousins and the younger apprentices.
S4.think: I'd feel good about it: in ten years I could run my own small crew with a couple of robots doing the heavy work. I'd rather own one robot than be replaced by somebody else's.
S4.do: Gets his ticket, grows the tree business and saves for a first robot by year five or six. Takes a part-time business course and proposes to his girlfriend next year as planned.
S4.feel: Calm and excited, as if he had a long runway.
S4.quote: I don't want my kids to think work is something that just happens to you.
S4.fieldNote: Colin sees a decade of warning as a runway to business ownership, robots included. His traditional values show in wanting children to see their father run something. He'd rather public money helped small owners buy machines than went to handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have the money or the ticket to buy in before the big companies took everything. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses and tradespeople to buy the new machines, so it's not only the giant firms that own them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether the robots would even be good at fire work. These hills are steep and rocky, and every fire season is different. I'd want to see a robot handle that before anyone pulls the people off it.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own one robot than be replaced by somebody else's.
portrait: Colin is a 27-year-old junior lineworker with a contractor fire-proofing power lines in wildfire country, still making rookie mistakes on a crew of veterans, with a weekend tree business on the side. He uses AI every day as his unpaid secretary and bookkeeper, holds firm free-market views and wants apprenticeships rather than handouts. He's calm in the plateau and steady disruption, seeing a race he can win. The two-year AGI picture frightens him privately, but he'd respond by buying an early robot and delaying his engagement. With five or ten years he plans to own a small robot-assisted crew, marry his girlfriend Rachel and raise children who see their father run something.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he wouldn't have the money or the ticket to buy in before big companies took everything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small businesses and tradespeople to buy the new machines, so it isn't only the giant firms that own them.
